title: Reception of the Classical Tradition in International Law: Grotius' De Jure Belli ac Pacis
author: Modern
content:
Essay

RECEPTION OF THE CLASSICAL TRADITION IN INTERNATIONAL LAW:
GROTIUS'

De Jure Belli ac Pacis

by

David J. Bederman
[*]

	Hugo de Groot, also known by his Latin eponym, Grotius, has been called the
"father of the law of nations."
[1]

Although
it hardly matters today whether he deserves such credit, his treatise, 
De
Jure Belli ac Pacis
 (On the Rights of War and Peace), first published in
1625,
[2]
 justifiably remains a classic.
His
book has been considered the first systematic treatment of international law.
Adam Smith, in lectures delivered in 1762 on the subject of moral philosophy
and the law of nations, said that "Grotius seems to have been the first who
attempted to give the world anything like a regular system of natural
jurisprudence, and his treatise On the Laws of War and Peace, with all of its
imperfections, is perhaps at this day the most complete work on the subject."
[3]
 Later writers have suggested that the
key
influence of Grotius' treatise was as a "systematic reassembling of practice
and authorities on the traditional but fundamental subject of the 
jus
belli
 [laws of war], organized for the first time around a body of
principles rooted in the law of nature."
[4]

	This essay will not attempt to assess Grotius' continued influence on the
development of contemporary international law. This has been ably done in many
different contexts.
[5]
 Nor will I
attempt to
appraise the impact of Grotius' natural law theories on his contemporaries.
[6]
 The thrust of this project is,
instead, to
determine the ways and means by which Grotius "reassembl[ed the] practice and
authorities on the traditional" subject of international law. My interest is in
understanding how Grotius used different kinds of textual authority in
constructing his systematic exposition of the rules of international law.

	Almost the entirety of this textual authority (at least for the 1625 edition
of the book) came from antiquity.
[7]

Those
sources can, in turn, be equally divided between biblical quotes and the
writings of classical authors. My consideration of Grotius' use of scripture in

De Jure Belli ac Pacis
 will have to await another day, although some
scholars
[8]
 have recently undertaken
this
examination. The focus of my contribution will, instead, be on the classical
Greek and Latin sources to which Grotius referred. I will examine here the ways
in which he used classical texts to recount instances of State practice in
antiquity and thus to construct rules of international behavior for States in
the early seventeenth century. My goal is nothing less than to explore how the
law of nations in antiquity, as reflected in classical texts, was received and
understood in early-Modern times. A reading of Hugo de Groot's 
De Jure Belli
ac Pacis
 is a good place to begin such a study.

I.  CLASSICAL TEXTS AND THE CICERONIAN 
HUMANI
GENERIS
SOCIETAS

	The extent and depth of Grotius' citations to classical sources in the 
The
Rights of War and Peace
 is staggering. My reading of the text indicates
that Grotius made specific references to at least 120 different classical
writers.
[9]
 These writers span
virtually all
of the classical canon, and include not only the prominent Greek and Roman
historians and jurists, but also quite a number of philosophers and poets.
Grotius' selection of source material, at least in its classical focus, was
certainly eclectic and diffuse.

	The reason for this was that Grotius sought to use classical materials not so
much to provide authority for fine legal points, but, instead, to offer
evidence of the practice and customs of ancient States. For the principles of
natural justice, which he believed guided State conduct in international
affairs, Grotius resorted to using scriptural interpretation. But for his
account of State practice, Grotius did not need to rely solely on Roman
jurisconsults, who were relatively thinly represented in his text. Indeed,
Grotius seemed to have a definitive bias against using, as authority, the texts
of leading legal schools, including the more contemporanenous civil and canon
lawyers.
[10]
 In short, Grotius was not
so
much writing a legal treatise as he was drafting a compendium of the rules of
international law as reflected in actual State conduct.

	Further analysis of Grotius' citations to ancient authorities indicate
substantial emphasis being placed on historical or narrative texts. Chief among
these were the works of Diodorus Siculus, Demosthenes, Livy, Plutarch,
Polybius, Tacitus, Thucydides, and Xenophon. These were certainly regarded as
being the leading classical historians. Notably absent in Grotius' book are
citations to Herodotus, Josephus, and Sallust. Of these, Grotius' three scant
references to Herodotus (in his 1625 edition) probably represents the biggest
surprise in his handling of classical historical texts.

	The next largest group of citations are those to the leading classical texts
on oratory, statecraft and political conduct. In this category I would include
Cicero, Pliny, Quintilian, and Seneca. Indeed, Cicero is the classical author
whom Grotius cites most often; Cicero makes over eighty appearances in the 1625
edition. In the next group of citations I would include mentions of
philosophical works, most notably those by Aristotle and Plato. Next are epic,
poetic, or dramatic sources, including those by Euripides, Homer, and Virgil.
In the last group are references to the Roman jurisconsults, Paulus and Ulpian.
That still leaves over a hundred other classical writers, for each of which
Grotius made a few, isolated references.

	De Jure Belli ac Pacis
 thus exhibited the mind of an extraordinary
scholar. Grotius was, after all, more than an international law publicist. A
child prodigy, he entered the University of Leiden at age 11, and was presented
to the court of King Henry IV of France and acclaimed "the miracle of Holland."
Grotius found time in his long life to write nearly sixty books in Latin,
ranging in subjects from theology and biblical criticism, to history,
philology, and poetry.
[11]
 He may well have
been the best-read man of his generation in Europe, the equal in many respects
of his fellow countryman, Erasmus.

	Grotius was, by disposition, a Romanist. Cicero was his favorite classical
author, and certain Ciceronian turns of phrase permeated Grotius' thinking.
Consider, for example, the very title of Grotius' project: 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
. This was a borrowing from what Cicero denominated as the Roman law
of nations (or at least that part of Roman law dealing with private law
relations with foreigners), the 
jus gentium
.
[12]

Although some modern writers
[13]
 have
indicated that Grotius proceeded from a historical mistake -- the 
jus
gentium
 was analytically distinct from a law of nations (
jus inter
gentes
) -- it hardly matters in the context of Grotius' understanding
of
ancient sources.

	Grotius conceived of international law as being a set of rules which governed
the conduct of peoples in distinct communities. For example, in the section of
his book dealing with the conduct of hostilities,
[14]
 Grotius opined on whether there was
a
generally accepted, universal rule against enslaving enemies captured in war.
He concluded that in wars amongst Christians this was so. Likewise, Muslim
countries followed the same practice 
inter se
. But the absence of the
rule in inter-faith conflicts indicated that such a rule lacked the status of

jus gentium
.

	Grotius' preoccupation with universal rules derived from right reason (the

sine que non
 of natural law) suggests that he was strongly influenced by
Cicero's notion of 
humani generis societas
, a "society of mankind rather
than of states."
[15]
 This phrase
appears in
a number of places in Cicero's works, particularly in 
De officiis
[16]
 and 
De finibus bonorum et
malorum
.
[17]
 Cicero may have
inherited this phrase, in
turn, from Stoic philosophers,
[18]
 a
debt
that Grotius himself noted.
[19]
 The
thrust
of many of these references was to establish rules of law which were universal
or near-universal in character.

	Consider, for example, Grotius' extended discussion of whether a belligerent
could seize title over territory from one in "possession of long standing."
[20]
 He concluded that such would be
considered
"as contrary to the common sense of nations."
[21]
 In support of this proposition,
Grotius
cited a typical collection of sources. He began with a passage from "holy
writ," followed by short paraphrases of Isocrates and Titus Quinctius. Next he
offered a reconciliation of discordant sources from Tacitus and Diodorus
Siculus. What concludes the passage is a quotation from Cicero, from his 
De
officiis
, asking rhetorically "what justice can there be in depriving an
owner of the land, which he has for many ages quietly possessed?"
[22]

	This structure and ordering of documentation was typical for Grotius. None of
the biblical or Greek historical sources purported to enunciate a general rule
of international legal relations -- one that would have made war for
territorial aggrandizement illegal. Those sources could only illustrate
specific instances where outrageous territorial claims had been rejected. One
such case was Antiochus of Syria's demands to territories in Asia Minor,
formally claimed by other Diadochi, on the strength of Alexander the Great's
conquests. Tacitus called these claims "obsolete pretentions" and Diodorus
dismissed them as "idle tales and fables."
[23]
 But these are merely, in Grotius'
view,
the conclusions of historians. Uncomfortable with such authority, Grotius felt
compelled to end his discussion with a more lawyerly (if also more oblique and
rhetorical) quotation from Cicero.

	This pattern is repeated throughout 
De Jure Belli ac Pacis
. A
proposition of international law is made. Historical "evidence" is then offered
in the form of scripture or of historians writing in Greek or Latin. Finally, a
legal authority is cited (and often quoted) to support the proposition. More
often than not, that legal authority was Cicero, although on some occasions the
views of jurists like Ulpian were substituted. This pattern was by no means
invariable. Grotius could use Cicero as just another citation, without any
particular emphasis.
[24]
 In some
instances,
Cicero provided the 
only
 support for the argument being advanced by
Grotius.
[25]

	Grotius' reliance on Cicero was emblematic of his substantial ambivalence
about the reliability of ancient sources in the enunciation of rules of
"modern" international law. In order to accord with his theories of natural
law, the rules governing State relations had to be 
both
 universal

and
 based on right reason. How did a scholar writing in the early
seventeenth century prove both elements in the creation of a customary
international law?
[26]
 Antiquity
provided
the raw narrative of international history. Greek and Latin texts, especially
of the breadth that Grotius consulted, provided him historical data for nearly
five centuries of authentic State relations. To have ignored such a wealth of
historical fact would have been foolish. If the ancient historical record was
clear in the depiction of certain rules of State relations, the element of
universality was certainly satisfied.

II. GROTIUS' CONSIDERATION OF ANCIENT SOURCES

	But that left open the matter of whether these rules of international law,
derived from ancient State practice, were binding on the nascent nation-States
of Grotius' early modern Europe. This question is essential to an understanding
of how the classical tradition of international law was received in our time. I
will consider here Grotius' use of ancient sources in defining three critical
problems of State behavior, doctrines that transcended time and place: how
ancient States made friends through diplomatic contact, how they made faith
through treaties, and how they made war within the limits of the law. The
purpose here is not, of course, to chart even the barest contours of doctrines
of international law in antiquity.
[27]

Instead, it is to see how the ideas of State relations were transmitted and
received in early-modern times.

	Additionally, I will consider here whether Grotius' use of classical citations
was a form of misdirection or cover for his appreciation and concern for very
current events in international relations. Some recent publicists have
suggested that the plethora of classical citations in 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
 was an elaborate intellectual smokescreen.
[28

]
I beg to disagree. It seems inconceivable to me that Grotius, as an exponent of
humanist jurisprudence,
[29

]
would refer to the classical heritage in law only to divert attention from the
current law.

	This is not to say that Grotius was an antiquarian -- far from it.
I will
submit that at least for the areas of international law I consider here (the
protection of ambassadors, the interpretation and enforcement of treaties,
declarations of war, and reprisals), Grotius often enunciated the doctrines of
law derived from classical sources in preference to late medieval or
Renaissance State practices. Although this study cannot possibly attempt to be
comprehensive in comparing classical and medieval sources for the early-Modern
international law, I hope by careful examination of selected passages in
Grotius' book to understand how he regarded the ancient experience of the law
of nations.

A.  
Making Friends: Friendship and Diplomatic
Immunities

	Essential to the creation of any body of international law was the willingness
of peoples to live in peace with their neighbors. Every State has had to
consider how "foreigners" would be admitted into its political community on
some basis of protection and parity. Likewise, every authentic State system
 -- whether ancient or modern -- has had to prescribe basic rules for
individuals in one polity to make friends with people in another jurisdiction.
In the same way, it has been essential to the ordering of international
relations throughout the ages that legal protections be granted to embassies
and ambassadors visiting from other countries.

	Grotius, writing in the early seventeenth century, was every bit as
precoccupied with this problem as were the classical writers he relied upon. In

De Jure Belli ac Pacis
, Grotius devoted an entire chapter to the Rights
of Embassies, upon which subject he concluded that "[a]lmost every page of
history offers some remarks on the inviolable rights of ambassadors, and the
security of their persons, a security sanctioned by every clause and precept of
human and revealed law."
[30]
 Grotius
wrote
with the knowledge that ancient peoples self-consciously elevated the status of
strangers. It had been well-noted that in ancient Greek and Latin, the terms
for "barbarian," "stranger," and "enemy" were originally synonymous.
[31]
 Aristotle could write, after all,
that
strangers were slaves by nature and could be hunted down like beasts.
[32]
 And yet, in the same pages of his
tract,
Aristotle could recite no less than three instances in which foreigners were
asked to restore law and order to Greek city-States wracked by civil
disturbance.
[33]

	It is precisely this ambivalence which pervades the ancient record of the
legal status and treatment accorded to strangers living in the midst of
cognizable political entities. Grotius acknowledged this when he wrote that:

Virgil has so clearly explained who are to be reckoned FOREIGNERS, that we need
not have recourse to lawyers, to understand what is so well expressed by the
poet, who says, "I look upon every country as foreign, which owns not the sway
of our sceptre." Aen. vii. 369.
[34]

Grotius was well aware that foreigners in ancient Greece and Rome were
routinely subject to reprisals.
[35]

Self-help measures were common to all primitive legal cultures, and they were
surely significant in some aspects of ancient international relations.
[36]
 As it turned out, however, the
availability and widely sanctioned use of self-help measures—which
would
be natural with any primitive legal society—conditioned the need for
a
response. The alternative chosen by the Greeks and Romans was purely legal: the
development of forms and institutions which could moderate the atavistic and
particularistic tendencies of atomized States, and elevate the status of
foreigners and visitors.

	The most important of these forms and institutions was the right of embassy,
correctly identified by Grotius as the cornerstone of the laws of peace, the
violation of which provided just cause for war.
[37]
 In Grotius' treatment of diplomatic
privileges and immunities, he repeats the classical dichotomy of this legal
subject: the right of embassy was the prerogative only of independent
sovereigns, but, once the right attached, emissaries were considered
inviolable.
[38]
 Greco-Roman diplomatic
experience gave Grotius the historical breadth in perspective to understand the
real normative power of rules of diplomatic conduct and the sanctions for their
violation. Some scholars have maintained, however, that ancient Greek
city-States did not have a cogent "theory of diplomatic
immunity . . . until the emergence of Roman power."
[39]
 And, ironically enough, only one
ancient
writer made such a claim. Cornelius Nepos, writing much later of events
occurring in the fourth century B.C., described two Theban envoys, who were
subjected to an arbitrary detention by a hostile third State, and objected to
their treatment "considering that they were adequately protected by the rights
of a legation, which it had been customary to hold valid amongst all
peoples."
[40]

	The words of the captured envoys were significant. If their declaration was
properly recounted—and there is, of course, substantial dissension
among
classicists whether it was
[41]
 -- they
were surely appealing to some notion of customary international law. Indeed,
they even said that they were relying on the practice of nations as a binding
("valid") norm for all nations. Despite suggestions that the extension of
diplomatic immunities had to be agreed upon by treaty in order to be valid,
[42]
 it seems that the preferable
understanding
of Greek diplomatic history is that there existed (at a minimum) an inchoate
custom of respecting the fundamental personal integrity of envoys. This notion
obviously begs the question of whether that custom had acquired the force of
law by virtue of the sense, shared by all actors in Greek international
relations, that the duty to respect diplomatic immunities was a legal
obligation, and not merely an expression of courtesy or hospitality. In the
same vein, King Philip II of Macedon, father of the famous Alexander, was said
to have told the Athenians that "violation of the rights of heralds and
ambassadors is regarded by all men as an act of impiety, and by none more than
by you."
[43]
 Although there is
emphasis in
this passage on the universal character of diplomatic inviolability, there is
also the sense of a purely religious sanction for the violator: the imprecation
of being "impious."

	The maltreatment of a visiting envoy was regarded by the Romans as a breach of
the 
hospitium
 extended to all guests and patrons, a violation of which
was a form of treason against the State. Moreover, envoys were considered the
personification of the sending nation.
[44]

Later codifications of Roman law made clear that harming a foreign envoy was a
violation not only of the Julian law on public violence
[45]
 but also of the law of nations.
[46]
 A Roman citizen who harmed an
ambassador
was subject to noxal surrender, a ritual by which the person was handed over to
the offended nation for punishment, thus absolving the Roman State from the
violation of the law of nations.
[47]

Cicero
made clear that the purpose of such a surrender (a kind of extradition) was to
free the State from a religious taint.
[48]

	Coupled with the expressly religious sanction of noxal surrender were
corollary civil sanctions. Even if an offended State refused the "sacrifice" of
the perpetrators, and returned them to Rome, they could be stripped of their
citizenship.
[49]
 In any event, these
unambiguous rules as to the protection of envoys were deemed by the Romans to
derive from the 
jus gentium
. Quintus Mucius, speaking through an extract
in Justinian's 
Digest
,
[50]

clearly stated that rules of
diplomatic immunity were part of the law of nations.
[51]
 In Livy's narration, after Tatius
(king of
the Sabines and a colleague of Romulus) had committed a gross outrage upon some
envoys of the Laurentes, the offended nation commenced proceedings "
iure
gentium
."
[52]

	Grotius, following Cicero and Livy, made clear that violation of the
immunities of ambassadors was an offense against the law of nations. What was
of concern to Grotius in drafting his chapter on the Right of Embassies was
whether, and to what extent, a host nation could punish a crime committed by a
properly credentialed diplomat. On this matter, Grotius discerned substantial
disagreement among legal authorities. The nub of the problem, Grotius noted,
was the tension between natural law and the law of nations:

[S]ome writers are of the opinion, that it is ONLY from UNJUST VIOLENCE, and
ILLEGAL CONSTRAINT, that the law of nations protects ambassadors. For they
imagine that their privileges are to be explained according to the common
principles of the law of nature. Others again suppose that ambassadors are not
amenable to punishment for ALL offenses, but only for such as amount to a
transgression of the law of NATIONS, the principles of which are of such
general extent, as to include the law of nature: consequently there can be no
offenses for which the ambassador is not punishable, except for those actions
that are made such by the positive rules of MUNICIPAL OR CIVIL
LAW.
[53]

Grotius concluded that "this right [the immunity of diplomats from local
prosecutions] cannot, like the law of nature, be established upon unchangeable
rules, but derives all its efficacy from the will of nations."
[54]
 The law of nations was distinct from
natural law to the extent that it was made positively by States. "To settle the
point therefore," Grotius said, "we must consider how far nations have agreed
among themselves upon these principles; the proofs of which can only be found
in the evidence of history."
[55]
 The
obvious
source for this "evidence of history" was classical antiquity.

	There were, to be sure, noted instances when the Greeks and Romans did not
observe the letter or the spirit of the law of diplomatic inviolability. As
with the Greeks, the Roman refusal to accord protection to enemy envoys seems
only to have occurred in life-or-death national struggles. During the height of
the Second Punic War, with Hannibal bearing down on Roman forces in Italy, the
city of Tarentum sent an envoy, one Phileas, to Rome. During his stay, he
contrived to procure the release of Tarentine hostages kept at Rome for the
purpose of ensuring his city's alliance in the war with Carthage. Phileas
bribed some guards, and the entire Tarentine entourage managed to escape, only
to be quickly recaptured. The Romans quickly put them all to death.
[56]
 Livy rationalized this Roman
violation of
the 
iure gentium
 by implying that Phileas was not really a properly
credentialed emissary.
[57]
 Grotius
endorsed
this result.
[58]

	In a similar vein, when Jugurtha was in Rome on a peace mission he was
protected from interference despite being in a state of war with the Republic.
Unfortunately, Jugurtha used his stay in Rome to have one of his Numidian
rivals, Massiva, murdered.
[59]
 A
member of
Jugurtha's entourage was implicated, and despite claims of immunity from
criminal prosecution by virtue of his diplomatic status, he was punished.
Sallust, in narrating these events,
[60]

seems to imply that the procedure was irregular and that, normally, rules of
diplomatic immunity would have protected Jugurtha's minion. But this was not a
normal situation; the offender was punished "rather for reason of equity than
by the law of nations."
[61]

	From all of this evidence, Grotius was able to conclude that an emissary was
absolutely protected from any type of criminal process or interference within
the territory of a receiving State.

[T]o try or punish ambassadors is contrary to the law of nations, which
prohibits many things that are permitted by the law of nature. The law of
nations, thus deviating from the law of nature, gives rise to these
interpretations and conjectures, which reconcile with the principles of justice
a greater extension of privileges than the law of nature strictly allows.
[62]
28 

Grotius' consideration of classical sources and the Right of Embassy --
with its attendant rules of diplomatic immunity and privilege -- was thus
premised on an evolving, positive law of nations. Although one might have
suspected that Grotius would have been strongly inclined to regard the legal
rules governing such a basic question as having been controlled by immutable,
natural law, such was not the case. Classical sources offered Grotius not only
the historical raw material for his analysis of international custom, but also
the key jurisprudential insight of rights based on an independent 
jus
gentium
.

B.  
Making Faith: Treaty Interpretation and
Enforcement

	Grotius' consideration of diplomatic immunities in 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
 was enlightening, although probably not very controversial. In
early-Modern Europe, even during the outrages of the Thiry Years War
(1618-1648), there were few documented cases of abuses inflicted on visiting
emissaries.
[63]
. The basic principles
of
diplomatic practice were well-established and safe from distortion. Less
certain was the status of treaties, the fundamental means by which States made
faith with each other and prescribed a positive law governing their relations.
Grotius was no doubt aware that when he was writing his tract in 1624, the era
of treaty law was about to begin. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648—the
first modern, comprehensive, and pan-European peace settlement—was to
revolutionize how international law would subsequently be made.
[64]
 Prophetic as always, Grotius
anticipated
this development with the inclusion of an extraordinary chapter in 
The
Rights of War and Peace
 on "Interpretation of Treaties."
[65]

	Grotius regarded this as a critical subject. After all, one nation's material
breach of a treaty was cause not only for the termination of the agreement,
[66]
 but also could be proper grounds for
commencing hostilities. In view of his admonition that treaties had to be
observed in good faith,
[67]
 it was
only
natural that Grotius would prescribe rules for the correct interpretation of
treaties:

Good faith, observes Cicero, requires that a man should consider as well what
he intends, as what he says. But as acts of the mind are not, of themselves
visible, it is necessary to fix upon some determinate mark, to prevent men from
breaking their engagements, by allowing them to affix their own interpretation
of their words. It is a right, which natural reason dictates, that every one
who receives a promise, should have the power to compel the promisor to do what
a fair interpretation of his words suggests . . . .
It is
for this very reason, that specific forms have been assigned for treaties,
which are to be drawn up in terms of unequivocal and certain meaning. The
proper rule of interpretation is to gather the intention of the parties
pledged, from the most probable signs . . . .
[68]

Grotius then proceeded to articulate basic rules of construction for
international agreements, canons that would be familiar to any modern publicist
considering the subject.
[69]
 The
difficulty
for Grotius was that he regarded the interpretive exercise for treaties to be
governed by natural law principles. In contrast to his discussion of diplomatic
immunities, Grotius considered historical evidence to be illustrative, not
dispositive, in this area of international law. "Natural reason" governed here.
To this extent, Grotius was dismissive of those who regarded civil law
standards of contract construction as binding between nations.
[70]
 Grotius' handling of historical
sources in
this part of his work was, as a consequence, very different from his treatment
of diplomatic law.

	The Greeks were the first ancient people to develop rules of interpretation
for treaties, in recognition of the certainty that any written text was capable
of ambiguity and disputed meaning. The use of ratification oaths and the
development of anti-deceit clauses was illustrative of this process. Yet, the
results were ambivalent. Greek treaties were not appreciably made more certain
in application, nor more binding in character, because of the additions of
these features. What made the ancient Greek preoccupation with trust relatively
novel in ancient international relations was that they chose to achieve it by
largely secular—and humane—means. This approach was endorsed by
Grotius.

	Quite a few Greek international agreements contained self-consciously styled
anti-deceit clauses. One recent philologist has concluded that nearly fifteen
percent (some 23 of 166) of all inscribed Greek treaties from the period 700 to
300 B.C. contained some kind of provision to avoid later fraud or trickery.
[71]
 Most of these anti-deceit provisions
were
found in defensive alliances (
epimachia
), offensive alliances
(
symmachia
), or in peace treaties.
[72]
 Typical of these generic clauses
were
commands that the parties observe the terms of the treaty "without trick," and
"not with craft nor with strategem."
[73]
 One
proclaimed that the cities "shall devise nothing about this oath, neither by
craft nor by any false pretext."
[74]

	One of the most famous interchanges in ancient Greek diplomacy concerning
sophistic interpretations of treaties was the Athenian defensive alliance of
433 B.C. with Corcyra against her former parent city, Corinth. This

epimachia
 was in arguable violation of the Thirty Years Peace signed in
445 B.C. between Athens and her allies and the Spartans.
[75]
 After all, Athens had covenanted not
to
make any hostile move against Corinth. The Corcyrans and the Corinthians both
made petitions to the Athenian assembly. The Corcyrans urged the conclusion of
the alliance and advanced a literal reading of the treaty with Sparta.
[76]
 The Corinthians argued that,
irrespective
of a technical reading of the Peace, an alliance with Corcyra (even one
defensive in character) would violate the manifest object and purpose of the 30
Years Peace. The Athenians decided that the terms of the Thiry Years Peace were
ambiguous as to the conclusion of an 
epimachia
 with a city at virtual
war with an ally of Sparta. They decided to proceed with the agreement,
[77]
 which, with later strategems, was
upgraded
to an offensive alliance against Corinth and resulted in the resumption of
hostilities between Athens and Sparta.

	This incident is obliquely referred to by Grotius in the section on treaty
enforcement.
[78]
 Grotius' verdict, at
slight
variance with Thucydides', is harsh against the Athenians. This ancient
illustration motivated Grotius, however, to finely nuance his rules of treaty
interpretation. Grotius suggested that the canons of construction for treaties
varied with the underlying character of the agreement.
[79]
 In interpreting "favorable" clauses,
those
which grant reciprocal benefits to both parties or which relate to the common
good, the broadest constructions should be used. "Odious" provisions, those
which are burdensome to one party only, should be narrowly construed. This
schematic was surely constructed by Grotius as a reaction to Greek attempts to
preclude sophistry in their treaty-making.

	Grotius was more inclined to follow Roman-era practices in constructing
treaties with very precise terms. He apparently regarded textual clarity as
superior to hortatory anti-deceit provisions. This preference is manifest in
Grotius' extended treatment of two 
cause célèbres
 of
ancient treaty interpretation.
[80]
 The
215
B.C. treaty between Hannibal and Philip of Macedon was far more encompassing in
its obligations than a typical, Hellenic defensive alliance. Yet, while not an

epimachia
, it was too heavily qualified to be a 
symmachy
 in Greek
practice. The care that was taken to draft its clauses was evident from the
inclusion of provisions extending the pact not only to the then current allies
of the respective parties, but also to any allies and subjects each might
subsequently acquire in Italy. This clause was needed because, while it was
clear that an alliance leader could bind its confederates to an offensive
arrangement, there was some doubt whether these terms could be applied
prospectively.

	Exactly this controversy had arisen between Rome and Carthage regarding the
proper construction of the peace treaty ending the First Punic War in 241 B.C.
Each had agreed that "the allies of neither party should be attacked by the
other."
[81]
 Carthage had made what the
Romans regarded as a sophistic interpretation of that earlier treaty by denying
that it applied to subsequent allies. In other words, the Carthaginians
seriously suggested that an after-acquired ally would be free to attack Rome or
its confederate without engaging the international responsibility of Carthage.
The Romans argued that if this had been the intent of the parties there would
have been a clause in the 241 B.C. treaty barring either side from acquiring
any new allies. Polybius reported this Roman refutation of the Punic
position.
[82]
 The force of the Roman
legal
argument must have persuaded the Carthaginians; by 215 B.C. (and their treaty
with Macedon) they had crafted a specific treaty provision to acknowledge this
interpretation.

	Grotius considered this entire incident as a definitive case study of
interpretation for "equal" treaties.
[83]

Grotius devoted so much attention to this transaction because it was largely
indicative of Rome's sometimes problematic history of treaty observance with
competing powers. Some have seriously suggested that the Romans regarded all
treaties as 
nudae pactiones
 as in private law,
[84]
 creating only moral commitments but
not
civil, binding obligations.
[85]
 The
better
view was that Roman treaties did have some kind of status as a binding
contract; the only question was how the Romans approached contract enforcement.
Aside from the well-known problem of making ransom agreements with pirates or
marauders,
[86]
 the Romans tended to
regard a
treaty made with an enemy to be binding.
[87]

But there are well-known instances in which the Romans made sophistic
interpretations of treaties. In one such case (probably an apocryphal tale),
the Roman general Quintus Fabeus Labeo made peace with King Antiochus of Syria,
whereby the King agreed to forfeit half of his fleet to Rome. It is reported
that Labeo cut each Syrian galley in half to effect the agreement, thus denying
Antiochus the use of all his fleet.
[88]

	More credible was the situation involving the peace treaty between Rome and
the Aetolian League of 197 B.C.
[89]

This
agreement had been intended to be a 
foedus
 between Rome and the Greeks
to break Philip V of Macedon's power. The Romans promised that all lands and
conquered towns in Macedon would go to the Aetolians. But the Greeks proved
feckless and defected to Macedon in the ensuing conflict. When the Aetolians
realigned with Rome in the final stages of the conflict with Macedon, they
claimed their right under the earlier treaty to occupy Thessaly which had
surrendered to the Roman army. The Roman general Quincitius refused the Greek
request, noting that the Aetolians had breached the treaty by earlier aiding
Macedon. In addition, because the Thesallian cities had surrendered to Rome,
and had not been "conquered" (
captae
) as the treaty required, there was
no obligation by Rome to hand them over.
[90]

	The outcome of this interpretive exercise was consistent with what transpired
if a truce (
sponsio
) was later disavowed by Rome. The only recourse that
could be had by the aggrieved nation was against the military leader who
sponsored the agreement.
[91]
 This rule
gave
rise to the Roman practice of noxal surrender (or 
deditio
) of
individuals who had made a 
sponsio
 which was later repudiated. The
first, and most famous, of these incidents was the affair at the Caudine
Forks.
[92]
 Occurring in 321 B.C., at
the
time of Rome's expansion into central Italy, a Roman army (under the command of
two consuls, Postumius and Veturius) was compelled to surrender to a Samnian
general, Caius Pontius. In the misplaced belief that generosity would seal a
peace between the Samnites and Romans, Caius Pontius agreed to spare the lives
of the Roman army if the consuls and men would agree to the conclusion of a
treaty between Rome and the Samnites, requiring Rome to withdraw from territory
taken. Postumius and Veturius took an oath before both hosts and then ordered
the Roman legions to pass under a trellis of spears, symbolic of Samnian
supremacy and mercy. Not fully trusting Roman scruples, the Samnians kept six
hundred hostages as surety.

	The Senate and People of Rome promptly disavowed the peace treaty. Speaking
before the Senate, Postumius suggested that he and Venturius

be surrendered to [the Samnites] by the fetials, naked and in chains. Let us
thus liberate the people from an obligation we may have had cause of imposing
on them; so that there may be no hindrance to your re-entering on the war
without violating either religion or justice.
[93]

Thereupon, a delegation of fetials conveyed the generals, stripped of their
clothes, hands bound, to the Samnite capital of Casdium. The 
pater
patratus
 declared: "Inasmuch as these men became sureties for a treaty,
without the sanction of the Roman people, and thus rendered themselves
criminally liable, I hereby surrender them into your hands, in order that the
Roman people may thereby be absolved from the impious offense."
[94]
 But the Samnite chief would have
none of
this nonsense. He returned the consuls and six hundred hostages, declaring that
if Rome wished to observe its 
bona fides
, it could either adhere to the
treaty or return its legions to the mercy of Samnite power. The Samnites were
even less impressed with Postumius' subsequent conduct; having declared himself
a Samnite (by virtue of his 
deditio
), he kicked a Roman fetial in the
groin in order to give the Romans a pretext for restarting the war.
[95]

	The 
deditio
 was Roman legal formalism at its best and few treaty
partners accepted the Roman offer of a sacrificial hostage. In 236 B.C.,
Caludius Clineas made a treaty with the Corsicans which was then violated. Like
the Samnians, the Corsicans declined to accept his

deditio
.
[96]

The Celtiberians of Numantia in 137 B.C. also refused to accept the noxal
surrender of Hostilius Mancinus, after he waged a disastrous campaign against
them and was forced to conclude a 
sponsio
.
[97]
 By the time Rome
repudiated the two 
sponsiones
 with Jugurtha in 111 and 110 B.C., they
did not seem much troubled with legal niceties. No 
deditio
 of the Roman
officials was even offered to the North Africans.
[98]
 Although the authorities disagree,
[99]
 the best view seems to be that by
the
first century B.C., the Romans no longer viewed 
deditio
 as a necessary
remedy for the violation of a 
sponsio
.
[100]
 Grotius affirmed
this view at numerous junctures in 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
.
[101]

	Grotius' engagement with the classical tradition of treaty-making had a double
aspect. The first was his belief that rules for construing international
agreements had to be derived from right reason. Treaties—as
international
contracts—were governed by the principle of 
pacta sunt
servanda
,
rules that were divined from natural reason. Grotius sought to articulate those
rules through rationalistic taxonomy,
[102]
 a
method that appears elsewhere in his book, particularly in his characterization
of different kinds of conflicts. From the classical tradition he was able to
create different empirical categories of agreements—"favorable" and
"odious"—and to then ascribe different rules of interpretation to
treaties
in each category. In this way, Grotius used the evidence of classical history
to fabricate an artificial reasoning for international law.

	The second aspect of Grotius' handling of ancient treaty materials was in the
recognition that there were legal qualifications to his natural law first
principle of good faith. Even the Romans, respected by Grotius as abiding by
the law of nations, were capable of sophistic interpretations and material
breaches of their international obligations. Grotius had a healthy distrust of
legal formalism, and the Roman law of foreign relations (the 
jus fetial
)
was replete with them, the incident at the Caudine Forks being only the most
egregious.

	In this one sense, Grotius distrusted the classical authorities, even those
from Rome which he clearly admired. But this suspicion did not translate into a
wholesale adoption of more recent modes of treaty construction and enforcement,
which were themselves notoriously vague and uncertain.
[103]
14 Instead, it reflected Grotius'
caution
in using classical sources of State behavior.

C.  
Making War: Jus Ad Bellum and Jus In Bello

	So far, my discussion of Grotius' treatment of classical sources and doctrines
of international law might be considered peripheral to what was the main thrust
of his book. Explicating the law of diplomats and treaties was secondary to
Grotius' primary task of developing the laws of war. This project had, like the
ancient Roman god Janus, two faces. The first was to form a cogent theory of
just war, 
jus ad bellum
, to explain those circumstances which justified
modern States to have recourse to belligerency. The second task was to proclaim
rules on the proper conduct of hostilities, 
jus in bello
, irrespective
of whether the war was just or unjust. This was a critical distinction, one
that Grotius resuscitated from St. Thomas Aquinas,
[104]
 St. Augustine, Cicero, and earlier
writers on just war theory.
[105]
2814
Grotius
found ample support for his construct of the laws of war in the classical
authorities.

	The declaration of war by one ancient State against another reaffirmed
nationalist impulses in religion. Whereas the reception of ambassadors
symbolically indicated accommodation and peace, the ritual for opening
hostilities celebrated exclusion and superiority. All ancient civilizations had
ceremonies which properly sanctioned war, involving two kinds of ritual
institutions: intrepreters of sacred texts and sacredotal colleges. These
customs centered around two distinct, but obviously interrelated, tasks. The
first was to decide whether war would be sacred, good, and just or if it would
be profane, evil, and unjust. The second role was to oversee the rites that
would invoke the gods' support for war, and to ensure victory.

	No ritual in ancient international relations was as solemn or as significant
as the decision to initiate hostilities. That choice was immediately confirmed
or denied by the nation's own deities. If the war was just, and the formalities
proper, then triumph would be forthcoming. If not, defeat and despair would
visit the State. In Greece and in Rome no scriptural text provided explicit
guidance for when war would be just or unjust. The custom for declaring war was
a ritual intended for any set of factual circumstances. This sometimes gave the
proceedings a very formalistic flavor. In epic Greece, the primary concern was
that compensation for injuries be correctly sought before the conflict began.
[106]
 For the Greeks, the justification
for war
was important, particularly where there was a violation of a sacred duty held
by a State.

	For Rome, it was the ritual and not the gravity of the offense that gave rise
to the declaration of war.
[107]
 The
Romans
craved regularity, and they fashioned a fabulously sophisticated ceremonial for
declaring war. Like the Greeks, the essence of the rite was the demand for
reparations from the foreign State, the 
rerum
repititio
.
[108]

According to Livy,
[109]
 the 
pater
patratus
 (the leader of the delegation of the Fetial College) appeared at
the frontiers of the offending nation, and said:

Hear, O Jupiter, hear, ye territories [naming the country in question], let the
law of heaven hear. I am the state envoy of the Roman people; I come, as their
ambassador, in all justice and piety, and let my words gain credence.
[Whereupon the specific request for reparation was made.] If I unjustly or
impiously demand those persons or those things to be given up to me [in cases
of a request for extradition or cession of territory], as the messenger of the
Roman people, then never permit me to enjoy my native country.

After a period of grace was granted, the 
pater patratus
 reappeared at
the frontier, remonstrated with the defaulting nation, and called on Jupiter
and Janus to bear witness to the injustice of the other State's refusal.
[110]

	The Roman formula for declaring war was an oath. The fetial swore upon it, not
only in his individual capacity but also as the personification of the nation.
The sanction for making an unfounded request for reparation was individual
privation for the messenger and, implicitly, defeat for Rome in the ensuing
conflict. The 
fetial
 who bore false witness in these solemn ceremonies
invited the anger of the gods, while Rome would have to fear the disorder that
defeat in war would surely bring. Declaring war and receiving envoys were
institutions which depended, for their sense of obligation, on the rituals that
preserved the ancient State against chaos.

	Grotius recognized that the classical mind regarded public war
[111]
 as the exclusive province of the
State,
entered into, as Cicero declaimed, only "after an official demand for
satisfaction has been submitted or warning has been given and a formal
declaration made."
[112]
. This
requirement,
Grotius believed, was rooted in natural law, and it was not necessary for its
proof to consult the actual practice of nations in creating customary
international law. Grotius' consideration of the laws of war—
restrictions on the ways and means of combat—was likewise premised on
natural law principles. The underlying purpose of these rules was to provide
succour and protection for the sick and wounded in war, combatants and
civilians alike. Grotius was undoubtedly reacting to the terrible excesses of
the belligerents in the Thirty Years War,
[113]
 which was in full swing at the
time of
his drafting of 
De Jure Belli ac Pacis
.

	Grotius gave careful consideration to the nature of reprisals in war and
protections afforded innocent parties. In one chapter,
[114]
 he drew the obvious parallel
between the
practices of ancient and modern peoples in subjecting the lives and property of
individuals to claims made by enemy States. Grotius also carefully reviewed the
Greek practice of 
androlepsia
,
[115]
 already discussed in this
essay,
[116]
 tracing its influence on
modern
doctrines surrounding maritime captures.
[117]
 Grotius considered the regulation
of
naval prizes as part of the public international law concerned with war and
neutrality, a subject that he had earlier opined upon in his legal brief, 
De
Jure Praedae
.
[118]
 Nonetheless,
Grotius was intensely critical of
ancient practices of reprisal, and he believed that they had no place in a
modern law of war which sought to protect the innocent. He saw this as a "law
of love,"
[119]
 part of the "natural
and
fundamental law of nations," although not necessarily recognized by the "civil
and conventional law of particular states."
[120]
 Here, at least, Grotius preferred
classical State practice to that observed in the middle ages, a time when
hostage-taking and reprisals were rampant.
[121]
.

	Indeed, a most notable synthesis of natural law and the law of nations occurs
in Grotius' chapter on the Right of Burial. Grotius placed these passages after
his consideration of diplomatic law, and he noted that "[n]ext to the right of
ambassadors Dion Chrysotom places that of burying the dead, and calls it a
moral act, sanctioned by the unwritten law of nature."
[122]
 "Moral act" or no, Grotius says in
the
same paragraph that "[t]he right of burying the dead is one of those
originating in the voluntary law of nations."
[123]
 Although Grotius acknowledged the
cognitive dissonance of the same act being required under sacred law, and yet
also being "voluntary" and subject to change under an evolving customary law of
nations, he concluded that "public enemies are entitled to burial."
[124]

	Grotius reached this conclusion in the manner already suggested in this essay:
he canvassed the ancient narrative sources. These, according to Grotius, were
unanimous in indicating that all enemies were to be accorded the right of
burial, except those who had committed suicide.
[125]
 But in his discussion of the
ancient
sources Grotius added an important methodological caveat:

As the ancients measured the moral character of every people by their
observance or neglect of these [burial] rights, in order to give them a greater
appearance of sanctity, they ascribed their origin to the authority and
institutions of their Gods; so that in every part of their writings we meet the
frequent mention of the rights of ambassadors, and the rights of burial, as
founded upon divine appointment.
[126]
14

Grotius seems to suggest that despite the consensus of practice in the
classical world on the rights of burial and embassy, the system lacked a
critical, rational component. Because the source of sanction in ancient
international law was limited to divine authority (or the acts of societal
institutions serving divine authority), the evidence of State practice in
antiquity could not be persuasive for someone attempting to deduce rules of
behavior for modern nation-States on more secular terms. That is why Grotius
notes elsewhere in his book that "[t]here is a precaution too necessary to be
given, against drawing too close a parallel between ancient and modern
times."
[127]

	People in antiquity conceived of three different kinds of sanctions applicable
in international relations. The first was divine sanction, based on a fear of
direct punishment by the god or gods invoked in an international undertaking.
The source of this compulsion was religion. Second, there was a social sanction
enforced through the rituals, institutions, and political legitimacy of the
ancient State, and manifested by a fear that the national god or gods would
abandon that State to its enemies. Custom was the source of this penalty. The
third was an intellectual sanction, developed through legal argumentation and
rhetoric, motivated by the fear of being deprived of a moral right and freedom
of action. Its source was reason.

	It would be a mistake, however, to regard these three sources of international
legal obligation as discrete impulses in the ancient mind. Religion mixed with
custom and reason to produce different combinations of sanctions in ancient
international relations. This should come as no surprise since, even in modern
societies, these constraints on human behavior combine in sometimes surprising
ways. It is rare that a religious tradition, which at its inception can simply
articulate commands for conduct, can long withstand forces which ritualize
belief and make it serve as a form of political legitimacy. Religion and custom
may also, after a time, become secularized. The sources of ancient
international law also experienced each of these transformations.
[128]

	Ancient international law was, at its heart, sanctioned by belief, but its
first principles were governed by ritual, custom, and reason. As a result, the
belief in enforcing good faith in antiquity was not exclusively a function of
religion. The classical sources that Grotius relied upon in 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
 suggested that the people of antiquity imagined different sources of
international legal obligations. Their fear of direct, divine retribution was
plainly religious. But their concern for maintaining social order was motivated
more by a dread of chaos, than of provoking the anger of their gods. Lastly,
rules of State behavior were also conditioned by pragmatism, reasons that were
not attributable to a fear either of divine vengeance or abandonment. Religion
was not, as Grotius supposed, the sole source of international legal obligation
in ancient times. Instead, religion and ritual and rhetoric mixed to produce a
concept of obligation which was premised on the first principle of ancient
international law: breaking faith brought punishment, whether godly or human,
immediate or delayed, terrible or trivial.

	This being settled, there remained the question, first posited by Grotius, of
whether it would have made any difference had ancient international law been
really religious in character. This inquiry only matters if Grotius had an
unstated assumption that a religious basis for international law was somehow
defective and dangerous. Yet Grotius clearly believed there was a place for
religion in supplying the moral sanction of legal obligation between States.
Yet, he was also concerned about the law of nations in antiquity being too
primitive, too remote, and too irrelevant for modern experience.

III.  GROTIUS' ENGAGEMENT WITH THE ANCIENT MIND

	Grotius' handling of international law accounts from antiquity reflected not
only his political philosophy, but also mirrored his generation's understanding
of the entire classical tradition. The confluence of these streams of thought
in 
De Jure Belli ac Pacis
 was critical in establishing it as a
ground-breaking work, a classic in the same sense as the sources that Grotius
cited. To understand the mind that wrote 
On The Rights of War and Peace
,
one needs to appreciate Grotius' moral outlook and his intellectual method.

	Grotius was conditioned by his belief that political
relations—whether
between individuals, communities, or States—were premised on moral
considerations. Grotius was encouraged by the advent of powerful nation-States
in Europe. Political orderings between peoples would be rationalized and
improved, and aggregations of communities into larger polities would improve
the chances of peace. Yet, despite these hopes, Grotius had to confront the
reality in both 1625 and 1646
[129]

that
these nation-States could also be the engines of immense destruction because of
wars carried on for religious or nationalistic impulses. Grotius' moral
imperative, indeed his entire reason for writing 
De Jure Belli ac Pacis
,
was to craft a system of rules for the emerging nation-State.

	Drawing on his immense knowledge of classical antiquity, Grotius offered three
paradigms of international political structuring. The first was the liberated,
chaotic, and utlimately self-destructive international life of the Greek
city-States. The second was the static and ordered 
imperium
 of the Roman
Empire. Grotius posited that both of these were unsuited for early-Modern
Europe; neither anarachy nor hegemony were desirable. The third model was the
early to middle years of the Roman Republic. This model represented a
nationalistic (but peace-loving) polity, one that had recourse to war only
after the most grave offenses and most solemn of ceremonies. This was the Rome
of Livy and Polybius, and (most importantly of all) Grotius' beloved Cicero.
Here was an example that could be taken to heart by the rulers of early-modern
States: Roman greatness, Roman order, Roman peace. This all resonated with
Grotius' love of the classical Roman tradition.

	There was only one problem with this classical construct, thoughtfully
imported for the modern statesman.
[130]
 It
was all a myth—and Grotius knew it. Well-read in classical history,
Grotius could have easily discerned that the Roman Republic was every bit as
atavistic as its neighbors, and that its international legal formalism was
often a cover for naked aggression. Nevertheless, this was the paradigm that
Grotius chose because it most closely matched the political conditions which he
observed in Europe in the early seventeenth century. Grotius knew that he had
to refashion the international history of antiquity and to place it in a
durable construct that would provide neutral sources for legitimate rules of
State conduct.

	The vehicle for this transformation of the classical experience was, as I have
already suggested,
[131]
 Cicero's
notion of
the 
humani generis societas
. By emphasizing a body of law for a "society
of mankind, rather than of states," Grotius could inject a moral element of
natural law as a counterweight to what were often regressive State practices
which formed the basis of the customary and "voluntary" law of nations.
[132]
 It is no surprise, then, that
Grotius
assigned varying significance to natural law dictates and to customary
international law evidences in his consideration of different international law
doctrines. When he was on safe ground, like the near-universal privileges and
immunities given to ambassadors, Grotius could emphasize the classical 
jus
gentium
 as a pure expression of State practice. There was no need to cloak
this area of international law under the guise of moral principle, nor even to
recount more recent trends in the law of diplomatic immunity. It was enough
that States observed certain international conduct, and one did not really need
to inquire why they did.

		But when Grotius considered more controversial doctrines, such as treaty
observance and initiation of hostilities, then the moral tone of his outlook
was most evident. This manifested itself as a distrust of certain aspects of
the classical tradition of State relations which he otherwise cherished, and by
recourse to scriptural citations. His embrace of Cicero's 
humani generis
societas
 led Grotius to discount what were clear and obvious examples of
particularism and national chauvinism in ancient State relations, traits which
dictated the workings of those State systems. Maltreatment of foreigners,
culminating in State-sanctioned reprisals,
[133]
 was only one aspect of that
classical
legacy, a legacy that Grotius chose largely to ignore or minimize as much as
was consistent with his defense of an international order based on powerful
nation-States. Understanding these problematic passages of 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
 forces the reader to reconcile Grotius' use of both classical and
biblical authority, as well as examples of more contemporary State practice.

	Understanding Grotius' world view
[134]
 is
not enough, however. There is the more subtle matter of the intellectual
approach to his subject. While the material that Grotius used for 
De Jure
Belli ac Pacis
 was classical or classicist, his scholarship was thoroughly
and unmistakably modern.
[135]

Superbly read,
Grotius had the depth of knowledge to collect vast amounts of material, and to
organize it in rational as well as novel ways. Throughout 
De Jure Belli ac
Pacis
 there is a dramatic tension in the ways that Grotius used classical
sources. His dominant approach was deductive, in that Grotius used evidence of
State practice in antiquity to propound rules of international law.
[136]
 His alternative second method was
inductive. On these occasions, Grotius devised a categorical approach to
characterizing State behavior, and then would fit the classical sources into
his preconceived hypothesis.
[137]

	Grotius eschewed formalism in the construction of international legal
doctrines, but he was also an unrepentant taxonomist. He purported to
scientifically approach the historical record of State practice, although he
was prepared to modify (and even distort) that evidence in order to fashion
rules of enduring significance to modern nations. Grotius thus embodied the
contemporary ambivalence of legal scholarship. He sought to balance the
legitimacy of law as descriptive science with its power as social theory.
Grotius' dilemma is familiar to the international law scholars of today:
divining rules which are descriptive of how States really behave, and yet, are
also binding on States irrespective of their will.

	Grotius must have believed that the contemporary law of nations was to be
fashioned only by the modern, rational mind. Classical antiquity may have
provided the raw experience of State behavior. But no known writer of that
period¾not even Cicero¾ had undertaken the task that Grotius had
assigned for himself. His accomplishment was the creation of a self-sustaining,
artificial reason for international law that could bridge the gap between moral
right (natural law) and State practice (custom).
[138]
 Grotius not only created a new
discipline
and gave it content, he achieved a rational intellect which would direct the
course of international relations, from his time to ours.
[139]
